draft.title: Analysing a narrative technique
card: Name
Say which technique the writer uses, such as symbolism, foreshadowing, a shifting timeline or a first-person narrator.
Example
Point to a moment in the text. Describe it in your own words or use a short quote.
Effect
Explain what the technique does to the reader, such as building dread, creating sympathy or making us doubt a narrator.
Link
Connect the effect to the text's ideas. This shows why the writer chose the technique.
draft.remember: Name it, show it, explain its effect, then link it to the idea.

a.q: A story opens with a cracked clock on a wall, and later the family falls apart. A student writes that the clock hints at trouble to come. Which technique is this?
opts: Foreshadowing
Flashback
Dialogue
First-person narration
a.why: An early detail that hints at later events is foreshadowing. A flashback would jump back to an earlier time, which the clock does not do.
a.clue: The detail hints at what happens later.

b.q: A student writes: The narrator is a child, which is a technique. Which addition best completes the analysis?
opts: It lets the reader see events innocently, so trust feels lost
It is a choice used in many stories for children
It shows the writer is skilled at writing
It makes the story longer and more detailed
b.why: A full analysis explains the effect on the reader and links it to an idea. The other options give no effect on the reader, or no link to the text's ideas.
b.clue: Say what it does to the reader, then tie it to an idea.

It is the weakest model of the 'effect then link' step the card teaches. Something like 'lets the reader see more than the child does, showing how innocence is lost' would be clearer.
The right option is the only long, specific one with a 'so' clause, so a student can pick it by its shape without understanding effect and link.

proposal.title: Analysing a narrative technique
card: Name
Say which technique the writer uses, such as symbolism, foreshadowing, a shifting timeline or a first-person narrator.
Example
Point to a moment in the text. Describe it in your own words or use a short quote.
Effect
Explain what the technique does to the reader, such as building dread, creating sympathy, or letting us see what a narrator misses.
Link
Connect the effect to an idea in the text. Without both effect and link, the analysis is not complete.
proposal.remember: Naming a technique is only the start. Its effect and link to an idea show why it matters.

a.q: A student writes: early in the story, a cracked clock hangs on the wall. This is foreshadowing. Which steps are still missing?
opts: The effect on the reader and the link to an idea
The name of the technique and an example
An example and the link to an idea
A short quote and the name of the technique
a.why: The student names foreshadowing and describes the clock in their own words, which counts as an example. They never say what the clock does to the reader or how it connects to an idea. A quote is not required, since a description in your own words also works.
a.clue: Has the student said what the clock does to the reader?

b.q: A student writes: the story is told by a child narrator. Which addition completes the analysis?
opts: We see more than the child, showing how innocence is lost
We see more than the child, so the plot is easy to follow
The theme is innocence, since the narrator is a child
Many writers use child narrators, so it is a common choice
b.why: The right answer gives an effect on the reader, seeing more than the child, and links it to an idea, lost innocence. The plot option gives an effect but no idea. The theme option names an idea but says nothing about the reader.
b.clue: Look for both something the reader experiences and an idea.
